rv.q: By staging it so effectively in pocket-sized form, Warchus may have inadvertently made a case for Martin Guerre as a minor piece rather than a rediscovered classic; it’s hard to imagine this iteration of the musical transitioning to a bigger stage.
Indeed, it plays out like a pacy, screamy folk-horror, but one that takes itself far too seriously.
What you’re left with is Leeds Mis, as a friend quipped.
I’m glad I’ve seen Martin Guerre — but, definitive or not, I found it intriguing rather than devastating, skilful more than soulful.
But it is, simply, not a great musical.
You betcha, without the tiniest soupçons of a doubt.
This trimmed-down revival makes a compelling case for a long-misunderstood work.
So, this updated version's heart remains elusive, but its undeniable charm keeps our blood pumping.
And yet, it still doesn’t quite earn its place among the golden greats.
The singing is great, but the tone is relentlessly dark, and you may struggle to follow the story.
This semi-staged production is an extraordinarily moving reimagining of the original musical.
The whole cast is fantastic; their voices are nothing short of angelic, and watching the play in the round really brings it all so very close.
It’s not that Martin Guerre is bad at all, it just struggles to work out that final step from goodness to greatness.
However, the repeated waving of large flags feels counterproductive in a production striving to emerge from Les Misérables’ shadow.
There is still a great deal to love about Martin Guerre, and it remains an amazing musical.
It is gripping in its own way, but it is neither epic, nor does it quite have the intimacy of a love story.

cn.t: Mixed reception for Boublil and Schönberg's reworked musical, which still struggles to escape Les Mis's shadow despite strong vocals and staging. Critics find it committed but emotionally underwhelming, questioning whether this "definitive" version finally works.
